BasePK: 2676401

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, we have
listened patiently to the arguments of all parties. I believe we should get information when we ask questions or put notices of motions on the order paper. The Creditistes certainly have not taken too much of the time of the House with notices of motions on the order paper.
I see that notice of motion No. 63 in the name of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin) has been on the order paper since November 25, 1969 and that nothing has been done about it. The Ralliement creditiste can certainly not be accused of wasting the time of the House in this field.
I will conclude by saying that whatever the number of notices of motions put on the order paper they all seem to get the same treatment.

BasePK: 2676661

Speech:
Mr. Chairman, clause 14(3) attempts to deal with an old problem. It attempts to settle a growing feeling on the part of Canadians that the vote in Canadian general elections ought to be reserved to Canadian citizens. This feeling became increasingly evident during the great period of postwar immigration. The idea has also become very popular among younger Canadians. We took some steps in this direction when passing the Citizenship Act of 1942, for example, which established who is a Canadian citizen. That act made it essential for anyone who wished to become a Canadian to apply for Canadian citizenship. It included a provision saying that a British subject who had been living in Canada for five years before the coming into force of the act would automatically become a Canadian citizen.
However, the dual nature of Canadian voting remained enshrined within the Elections Act. It has remained there to this day, much to the annoyance of the hundreds of thousands of immigrants who have come to this country from non-Commonwealth countries and who, while waiting their five years to become Canadian citizens, saw other people coming from Commonwealth countries enjoy the privilege of participating in federal elections, even though they had been here for only one year. It is, therefore, reasonable for us to see expressed in amendments to the Elections Act a desire to cure an old anomaly.
Canada Elections Act
The trouble is that the bill would not do that. The act we are considering simply entrenches the rights of a class of non-Canadian citizens who will have the privilege of voting until they die. It says that every British subject, other than a Canadian citizen, who was qualified as an elector on June 25, 1968 is deemed to be qualified as an elector.
This provision simply means that a person, let us say, who was 21 years old at the last election and qualified to vote, may continue to vote without ever becoming a Canadian citizen for as long as he lives, perhaps for 40, 50 or 60 years or more. So, if we pass this clause, we shall be creating two classes of British subjects in Canada, namely, those who by virtue of this act will be allowed to vote from now until they die, and those other British subjects who will not have the privilege of voting until they become Canadian citizens. In addition, we would have a third class of Canadian citizens who would have the vote. I sympathize with those who believe that the vote should be reserved to Canadians. I believe that is what we ought to be doing.
On the other hand, I do not feel that by passing any clause of this bill we ought to cut off people from the franchise who now have the right to vote. I am not in favour of taking away immediately the right of those who have enjoyed the franchise. I think there is a way around the difficulty, and that way was hinted at by the hon. member for Skeena who spoke a few moments ago. He suggested that we should provide those who have enjoyed the privilege of voting by virtue of their British citizenship with the opportunity to become Canadian citizens, and that we should not disenfranchise them by accepting certain amendments. I, therefore, wish to propose an amendment to subclause 3, by substituting for line 10 on page 24 of the bill the following:
will be deemed to be qualified as an elector for a period not exceeding five years from the date of proclamation of this act.
Simply put, that means this: every British subject who is not a Canadian citizen and who was qualified as an elector on June 25, 1968, will be deemed to be qualified as an elector for a period not exceeding five years from the date of the proclamation of this Act. By accepting this amendment we shall take no voting rights away from anybody. We shall provide ample opportunity for British citizens to vote in by-elections which may occur between now and the time of the next general election, to vote in the next general election and vote perhaps in the election

June 17, 1970
Canada Elections Act
beyond that. But the warning is clear in the act. They will be asked to acquire Canadian citizenship, as is now the case for Poles, Germans and so on, many hundreds and thousands of whom live in my constituency. They will be asked to acquire their citizenship in order to vote in the next federal election.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I appeal to those who wish to strike out subclause 3 not to strike it out and deprive some people of their vote. That is not what Canadians want. We do not want to do something vindictive to those people who have come here and who have been given that privilege. Let us recognize that Canadians want the vote to be fair. Let us issue the warning within the Act. These people should be given an opportunity to become Canadian citizens and, after a reasonable lapse of time in which to acquire their citizenship, to vote.

Order, please. I quite agree with the Leader of the Opposition. That is not his point and that is certainly not the way I understood his argument. His argument is based more on a question of principle and propriety and, as the hon. member for Edmonton West said, the matter of an hour's gain or an hour's loss is not necessarily the substance of the argument which has been proposed by the Leader of the Opposition in opposition to the motion.
June 18. 1970

Motion to Extend Hours of Sitting
I suggest, with respect, to hon. members who have raised this point of order that the arguments brought forth are arguments in opposition to the motion itself. It seems to me that the motion should be put and that hon. members have brought arguments against it to the effect that in their view the motion should not be put and they would like to vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am not sure whether the minister was referring to me, but I did ask him a question about his speech last night. These two paragraphs have the effect of permitting a party label to be put on the ballot, or they permit a candidate to be described as an independent. I think all of us would agree that where the names of candidates are similar or confusing, some provision should be made for placing the party label on the ballot. Although the provision is permissive in its terms, the result in practice will be

that the party label will go on the ballot in all circumstances. This raises a question as to whether the practice is really desirable.
It is my contention that if the names are not confusing it is undesirable that the party label should appear on the ballot. My reasoning is this: there has been a tendency in recent years for political parties to be merchandised much in the same way as commercial products. However, one great problem in carrying out a successful merchandising effort has been that at the point of sale, namely, the polling booth, the party label has not been in evidence. This means that a candidate during the election has an extremely important function to perform, which is to make known to the electors that he is the candidate for a particular party. If the party label were allowed to appear on the ballot it would mean that the central organization, having the benefit of large election funds and having access to radio and television coverage, would be able to merchandise the entire party; there would be no need to get individual assistance from the candidates in establishing the connection between the large-scale merchandising effort carried on by the central office and the candidate in a particular constituency. In other words, the functions and the responsibility of a candidate would be greatly diminished.
My suggestion is, therefore, that party labels should not appear on the ballots as a general rule. If the vital function of the ordinary candidate in an election campaign were diminished it would mean that the importance of individual Members of Parliament would likewise be reduced; the degree of independence they possess would be lessened.
If there is any support for my proposal, I would move that paragraphs (h) and (i) of subclause (2) be deleted and replaced by a provision which would permit party labels to be used when there was some good reason for doing so, for example, if names of candidates were similar or confusing. Mr. Chairman, one of the difficulties about the proxy voting system is the increased risk of loss of control, in the sense that there may be loss of assurance of the relative fidelity of the voting system. There are two principles involved here. The first is the principle which motivated the hon. member to give to the maximum number of people the opportunity of voting in an election. There is, on the other hand, the generally desirable attitude that controls over the voting system should be relatively efficacious and that so far as possible we should prevent fraud, personation, and so on.
The problem with personation under our present system exists normally where individual A, knowing that individual B is an elector on the list of a poll and has not yet gone to the poll, goes to the polling station and represents himself to be B and votes in his stead. That is a simple case of personation. The protection against this-I acknowledge it is not very effective protection in the case of an urban poll-is the possibility that he will be recognized by someone at the poll as not being the individual he holds himself out to be. There have been a number of such cases in recent years.
The problem of proxy voting is that there is the risk of personation at one stage further; that is to say, an individual may go to a poll and represent as to a document, on which he or someone else may have forged the signature of an elector, that that is the signature of the absent person. It is difficult at the best of times to know the identity of an elector at an urban poll or, for that matter, at a rural poll and very few people-I think hon. members will recognize this from their own experience-will know the exact signature of an elector. So there is a greater risk of personation in such circumstances. For that reason I understand the committee confined itself to a relatively limited number of situations where it would be physically impossible for individuals to attend at the poll and they would have to appoint an agent for this purpose.
The case which had the greatest appeal for me and for the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, because of a common friend, was that of persons who because of illness or physical incapacity are incapable of leaving their residence and going to the poll. There you would be least likely to have a case of personation.

I therefore had an opportunity of reflecting on the general proposal and looking through this and the consequential amendments. As I indicated on second reading, the Ontario election law provides a certain amount of vouching in urban polls, particularly related to the fact that a person's name may be on a previous municipal list which provides certain evidence of local residence.
I was in favour of the motion as far as extending the privilege to urban voters was concerned. My colleagues have expressed concern. I suppose one's attitude in this regard is dependant upon local experience. I personally have not found any difficulty with the Ontario law, and I find vouching feasible under some circumstances. Some of my colleagues have doubts in this regard. Therefore, I have to approach any voting proposal from the standpoint of whether the concerns expressed to me can be met. There are two difficulties, particularly with reference to his analogy to passport applications. A person attesting to a passport application is required to attest not only as to his knowledge of the individual but to having known the individual for at least two years. In this case there is a situation whereby an individual would present himself to a minister, barrister, dentist, school teacher, bank manager or chartered accountant and say, "I am John Jones. I live at this address, which is in this constituency. I ask you to attest for me in this poll". Unless a person in one of those categories has actual knowledge of the individual's identity and place of residence, if he were a careful person he would say, "You may be both of those things, but how can I be sure? In view of the penalties involved, I do not propose to take that risk". That is what a person in that category would be required to say with regard to a passport application. Unlike normal vouching in a rural case, this is not a case of someone who enjoys propinquity, such as a neighbour or relative. This is a stranger picked from a list. He may not live close to the individual, and for that reason may not be able to attest to his identity and normal residence.
I agree this provision would assist in a limited number of cases where a barrister, bank manager, principal or mayor of the town happened to be a neighbour and could attest to these facts. In a large number of cases that would not apply. The amendment does not get around the basic problem of vouching in urban polls; that is the problem of the anonymity of the city, the fact that people do not necessarily know their neighbours. The difficulty arises when it comes to deciding who should be added to the list, bearing in mind the need to protect the system. My inclination would be to vote against the proposal even though I am concerned that the urban voter is placed at a disadvantage by reason of the absence of the vouching power.

When I moved this amendment initially, I stated quite clearly that I was not absolutely married to its wording and contents. I was attempting to make the point that electors in urban polling divisions whose names did not appear on the list should have an opportunity to cast their ballots on election day after being vouched for by someone else.

This official may be approached by a person who is qualified to vote and whose name is not on the list. After swearing an oath he is given a certificate which he takes to the polling station, accompanied by another person whose name is on the list for that polling division. The latter vouches for him and he is then able to cast his ballot. I agree there may be difficulties in very large communities in connection with this procedure since it might be impracticable for people to travel long distances to the office of the returning officer, but this is not an insurmountable problem.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that section 31 of the act must be repealed, and therefore that this amendment must be defeated. In essence, section 31 provides that if there is closure of an inshore fishery anywhere in Canada, there cannot be an offshore fishery with respect to the same species of fish. No long-distance fishing nation could possibly tolerate a provision of that character in its legislation. The amendment which we propose in the bill would allow a Canadian offshore operation to take place when there was an inshore closure somewhere in Canada.
Unfortunately, an example was given in the Standing Committee with respect to lobsters on the east coast. It was unfortunate in the sense. We have no intention of issuing regulations permitting an offshore lobster fishery. I have said this in a number of letters, not only to hon. members opposite but also to fishermen and their representatives in Nova Scotia. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we have no intention of upsetting the inshore lobster fishery in the Maritimes. I guarantee it.
I have also said that we would welcome submissions by the industry and a full-scale debate by the House of Commons all-party committee on Fisheries and Forestry when the House reconvenes in the fall.
I contend that to prohibit any long-distance offshore fishery because of a closed inshore fishery is short-sighted. From time to time hon. members ask, "Why doesn't Canada have an effective long distance fishing fleet?" Section 31 provides:
No one shall leave any port or place in Canada to fish outside Canadian fisheries waters...and no one shall bring into Canada any fish caught outside Canadian fisheries waters when fishing for such fish is prohibited inside the Canadian fisheries waters-
Clearly, if section 31 were to continue in effect we could not have a long-distance fleet carrying on an offshore operation when an inshore operation was closed. It is an anomaly in the Fisheries Act. If we have any idea of creating a long-distance fishery we get rid of section 31.

Fisheries Act

The Fisheries Act is almost as old as Confederation. It has served Canada and Canadians well in the century that has passed, since it has seldom required amendment. On the other hand, by reason of the amendments made in the 1960-61 session the Fisheries Act is unique among the laws on our statute books. Those amendments brought the act into conformity with the Canadian Bill of Rights by removing the provisions which violated human rights and fundamental freedoms. The Fisheries Act can be said to be the "Drybones" of the Revised Statutes of Canada. We had hoped to make the Fisheries Act the sovereign legislative speardhead against pollution of Canada's waters, including seacoast and inland, salt and fresh water. The Fisheries Act has everything going for it to carry out this role effectively. I say this because the constitutional power of this Parliament to control water pollution under the seacoast and inland fisheries provisions and the provisions of the British North America Act is exclusive and cannot be challenged.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43 I intend to ask the House for unanimous consent to present a motion on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity. In accordance with the rule, I now explain the basis of the urgency which compels me to seek this leave. 

A most critical situation has developed since the House adjourned last June; it is caused by the unilateral action of several provinces to prohibit, through marketing legislation, the entry into such provinces of farm products from other provinces. Such action appears to be clearly unconstitutional, particularly under Section 121 of the British North America Act; however, a judgment of a provincial court has upheld the prototype of such provincial legislation. A final appeal of this judgment may take many months. Meanwhile, other provinces have indicated they will pass retaliatory laws. There is now a drastic interference with the economics of the agricultural industry which may spill over into the other primary industries and the manufacturing industry as well.
The Prime Minister, with respect to the agricultural crisis, indicated that the passage of Bill C-197 would by itself provide the solution, that there was n>o need for a constitutional reference to the Supreme Court of Canada to settle the matter once and for all. He was wrong on both counts. With the failure of the government to bring in an acceptable bill which would be passed by Parliament this session and accepted by the provinces, it is now absolutely essential that there be an immediate reference to the Supreme Court. I therefore ask the unanimous consent of the House to propose, seconded by the hon. member for Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth), the following motion:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is essential that the government of Canada, upon consultation with the provinces, frame terms of reference under section 55 of the Supreme Court Act to secure the opinion of the court as soon as possible on the important constitutional questions raised by action taken by certain provinces attempting to prohibit the entry into such provinces of agricultural products from other provinces.

It is also proposed under the motion that the special $500 deduction allowed to taxpayers of 70 years or more be made available to pensioners at age 65. In 1965 the eligible age for receipt of the old age security pension was reduced from age 70 to age 65. This important change added substantially to the cost of providing that pension. The government decided that, rather than impose new taxes, part of this additional expenditure would be off-set by withdrawal of the special $500 deduction from those individuals under age 70 who received the old age pension. In this way again those most in need of the pension, because they had little or no other income, would receive the full benefit of the

pension while those with higher incomes would pay back part of the pension through taxation. All new recipients of the pension, except those with very high incomes, were better off because of receipt of the pension even though they gave up the special $500 deduction.

Such an individual could delay applying for the pension until the beginning of the following year and thus retain the $500 deduction for the year in which he became eligible for the pension.
A deduction based on age is not a very logical or precise way to provide tax relief. Some individuals over age 65 or 70 have large incomes. A deduction of $500 provides a much larger amount of tax deduction for a person with a high income than for a person with a low income.

If we were to look at the motion before us I think the hon. proposer would agree with me that the government should give consideration to improving the economic and social status of certain of Canada's senior citizens.

He says of all of Canada's senior citizens. The net result of his proposal has been to enunciate the disparities at almost every level because he speaks generally of each class in the same way.
I find it rather strange that the party with which he is affiliated would allow him to put forward a motion of this kind, bearing in mind that their stated purpose in life is to bring about a gradual egalitarianism in society. The net result of this motion, however, is to bring about wider disparity.
First of all, let us look at the increase in income tax exemption of $2,000 for single persons and $4,000 for couples. That means the person who is earning $2,200 and the person who is earning $50,000-very few might be earning $50,000 so let us say $25,000 because there are many in the public service today earning $25,000 a year-would get the same benefit at the marginal rates. The difficulty in increasing exemptions is that the effect is at the marginal rate of the taxpayer. Taxpayers with a 50 per cent marginal rate-in this particular instance a married couple-would receive a benefit of $1,000. A person earning $3,000 or much lower, where the marginal rate is much less-it could be as low as 15 per cent-would receive a mere pittance.
That is why the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mahoney) stated I have long advocated that greater equity could be achieved through a tax credit system. Unfortunately the government has not seen fit to follow this suggestion. I maintain that greater justice would be achieved with a tax credit system, notwithstanding the fancy arguments advanced by government experts with regard to difficulties in connection with tax credits, and that they could do better by raising the exemptions. I remain unconvinced, as I think most people do, that greater equity would be achieved by increasing the exemption proposed by the government.

Mr. Speaker, June 20, 1969, and again May 4 of this year, were days allotted to the opposition and they chose to deal with the subject of veterans pensions.
This is a worthwhile and welcome debate because it reflects the interest of members of all parties in the human side of the question. In all the years that I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs-and that dates back to the time when the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) was the committee chairman-I have seldom encountered partisanship when the needs and the wellbeing of war veterans were being considered.
It may be useful to put on the record the introduction to the government's white paper on veterans pensions. It reads in part as follows:
For the past 50 years, Canada has recognized and freely accepted her obligation to pay compensation for disability and

October 27, 1970
Veterans Allowance Increases
death arising out of military service, in so far as it is reasonable and practicable to equate monetary values with human suffering and bereavement.
This is done through the Pension Act, the keystone of Canadian veterans legislation since 1919. It provides for the payment of pensions to the disabled veteran, his widow and his orphan, and to his dependent parents, sisters and brothers.
In addition, an award of pension also makes the recipient or his family eligible for other benefits. The veteran himself becomes eligible for medical treatment for his pensioned condition, special re-employment training if he needs it, war veterans allowance, and funeral and burial grants. After his death, his widow is eligible for war veterans allowance, and his pensioned children for advanced educational assistance.
The veterans of Canada comprise about one twelfth of the country's total adult population. Approximately 832,600 of these are veterans of World War II (or of both wars or of Korea) and another 112,600 are veterans of World War I. Of these two groups a total of 136,800 veterans were in receipt of pensions under the Pension Act as of December 31, 1968, and a further 29,800 pensions were in payment to the dependents or survivors of veterans.
[DOT] (4:10p.m.)
For many years the Pension Act and the Pension Regulations which preceded it, have provided that pensions should be related to earning power; and the adjudication of pension claims has been the responsibility of an independent and impartial tribunal.
While adhering strictly to these basic principles, successive governments have found it necessary to review and amend the act in one way or another. Indeed, there have been few years during the half century when some change hasn't been made to the act.
The government is indeed aware of problems affecting war veterans, as well as thousands of other Canadians, and it is doing all that is possible to meet the situation in a rational way. There is no reason to assume that it has not kept faith with our comrades.
With regard to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I shall not find great difficulty in supporting it. I recall the statement that he made during the debate on June 20, 1969, when he voiced the suspicion that the government was going to draft legislation in advance of hearings on the Woods Report. We all know how wrong he was in his assessment, Mr. Speaker.
As pointed out by the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs held 39 meetings and heard witnesses from no less than 19 veterans organizations. I wish at this point to name the principal ones: The Royal Canadian Legion, the Army, Navy and Air Force Veterans in Canada, the War Pensioners of Canada, the Sir Arthur Pearson Association for War Blinded, the Canadian Paraplegic Association, the Canadian Corps Association, the Nursing Sisters' Association of Canada, the National Dieppe Prisoner of War Association, the Hong Kong Veterans Association of Canada, The War Amputations of Canada, the National Council of Veterans Association in Canada, the Nationally Chartered Veterans Organizations, etc.
The Committee examined in detail each of the 148 recommendations of the Woods Report and, of course, all the proposals contained in the White Paper were closely scrutinized. The long and laborious study of the White
Paper, which kept the Committee working several weeks during the summer parliamentary recess, is evidence that the members of the committee took their responsibilities seriously. When the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis), Chairman of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs, presented the report to the House, its members had reason to feel that a good job had been done. It was a good report upon which, no doubt, legislation will be based.
One cannot exactly blame the government for the delay in the implementation of the recommendations contained in the report, because a great deal of work is involved in the preparation of such a complicated piece of legislation. Moreover, this very small income is very badly divided, which explains why many farmers survive only through chronic debts and social welfare allowances.

From 1951 to 1956, in Eastern Canada, 31,000 family farms were abandoned or sold for ridiculously low prices, which barely allowed second, third or fourth generation farmers to pay off their debts.

One of
the worst features of the bill is the retroactive provision that makes a person liable for punishment by reason of his membership in an unlawful organization even when that organization was not unlawful. This means that a young man who five years ago attended meetings of the FLQ but who has had no association with them since can, under clause 8, be arrested-and the onus would be on him to prove that he was not a member of the FLQ. He may be liable for five years imprisonment.
This retroactive feature I submit, Mr. Speaker, is in complete contravention of the declaration of human rights passed by the United Nations, a declaration to which Canada is a signatory. In article 11 of that Declaration of Human Rights, clause 2 says that no one shall be held guilty of any penal offence on account of any act or omission which did not constitute a penal offence under national or international law at the time when it was committed. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, in view of the editorial comments which have been made in newspapers right across Canada, that the minister would be well advised to re-examine this retroactive feature in the legislation. I can assure the minister that if he does not, we in this party will bring in amendments to give the House an opportunity to express itself on that question.
The legislation still retains the reverse onus which requires a person to prove, under certain circumstances, that he was not a member of an organization. That is in violation of the customary legal provision that everyone is considered innocent until proven guilty. This legislation-let us face it-provides for detention without charge, custody without bail and search without warrant. These are serious abridgements of civil liberties. We have asked repeatedly in this party, as have other members, that there be some provision for a commission of nongovernmental people who would have the right to see those detained, make sure that their rights were being safeguarded, that they were obtaining the services of legal counsel and that they were not being ill treated or subject to coercion or duress.
I think we have to question whether such restrictive legislation is required in a situation which the government itself contends no longer constitutes an insurrection. I think Parliament should grant the police the powers necessary to apprehend terrorists and kidnappers, but I do not think the government has shown us that it needs powers as wide and as repressive as those which are contained in this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, we recognize the need for legislation to deal with the situation arising out of the terrorist activities of the FLQ. Public Order Act, 1970
operate. Third, we are prepared to vote in favour of this bill on second reading so that it can be dealt with in Committee of the Whole. We hope at that time the government will be prepared to accept amendments that will modify some of the more arbitrary and restrictive provisions of the bill.

When a person is investigated without his knowl-

November 9, 1970

edge, hearsay evidence creeps into such a report, he is never presented with a copy of it, and for reasons never made known to him his contractual ability is affected. I think that, per se, is grossly unfair.
More and more we are coming to consider the protection of the privacy of the individual, making it the subject matter of modern legislation. More and more we are aware of the fantastic and overwhelming power of not only government but of bodies corporate acting in the commercial field within our society. Certainly, last year in the Justice Committee we spent a great deal of time on the invasion of privacy by electronic devices. Many provincial governments have passed legislation dealing with the subject. It is interesting to note from the Speech from the Throne that we can anticipate legislation along that line from this government.
In conjunction with this matter I would like to consider the problems pertaining to the storage of information about the person, the ability of machines to consolidate tremendous amounts of information about one person or many persons and to make it readily available throughout the world. Control of these machines and the organizations behind them must be a matter of great concern. One frightful aspect of this which is in the minds of us all is that of "Big Brother". As George Orwell wrote in "1984", the concept of government completely overshadows the privacy and right of the individual. The prospect of international corporations and multiconglomerate corporations having access to these data banks and the like which could so affect the individual in his daily life, is rather frightening. I think it is something with which we are concerned now and must be concerned about in the future.
As I have suggested, this resolution is relatively narrow in that it deals only with a very minor problem in relation to the whole issue. I have doubts about several aspects of the resolution. First of all, it has been suggested that it is a question that should properly be put in the hands of the federal government from a constitutional point of view. Certainly, it might be said to come within banks and banking, but it would not affect the many financial institutions which are subject only to the laws of the provinces in which they operate. Nor would it affect protective agencies which are under the law of the provinces and which so often find the information about which the hon. member complains.
It is certainly questionable whether it applies to the criminal law, though it is probably closer to that than any other aspect of the powers of the government of Canada. In that respect I am inclined to the view that it is far closer to provincial powers than to the Constitution. For my part, I am inclined to suggest that a resolution of this nature be left with the provincial government. In any event, the revelation of the material contemplated in the resolution might well be libellous and actionable if the motives of the person releasing it were not bona fide under the circumstances. I think it would be improper, under certain circumstances, to release such information even if it were the truth.

We support the amendment. We would have moved a similar amendment ourselves but we knew the hon. member for York South had put one down. The argument advanced by the minister would be fascinating if put forward before an appellate division, especially if the minister were arguing on behalf of the Crown that the words "on behalf of" were wide enough to catch people who communicated statements when they could not be proved beyond reasonable doubt to be representatives of the association. But there are two aspects of the bill which ought to be taken into account when evaluating the minister's statement.
It is not a question under this legislation of facing a charge, getting out on bail and then having a fine academic argument in a case where both the accused and the Crown are represented by counsel. In clause 9, we see what can happen to a person or an individual who is charged with communicating statements on behalf of an association. He can be picked up and detained for the period provided in the legislation. This takes him out of this fine, academic consideration of what the law is and whether or not he can be convicted. The second point is that in normal circumstances one could get into a fine academic argument concerning the burden of proof, mens rea, the necessity of an offence being proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the weight of evidence. But there is in this legislation an evidential clause which provides that communication "on behalf of" is assumed to be an offence though there is an opportunity for an accused person to prove his innocence. Clause 8 makes this provision beyond any shadow of a doubt. It reads:
In any prosecution for an offence under this Act, evidence that any person, either before or after the coming into force of this Act... communicated statements on behalf of or as a representative or professed representative of the unlawful association . .. is, in the absence of evidence to the contrary proof that he is a member of the association.
So, there are two retroactive aspects to this bill. I understand that this may be necessary. This is extraordinary legislation and I recognize it as such, but when we come to consider the amendment before us, provisions of the type to which I have drawn attention must be taken into account. Obviously, the government did take these things into account, because when we look at the regulations which were promulgated under the War Measures Act we find precisely the same wording as to the definition of the offence in clause four. But when we come to the question of the evidential aspect, it appears that the government had second thoughts because the words "on behalf of, or" are omitted and we find in 8(c) of the regulations under the War Measures Act the words "communicated statements of the unlawful association as a representative or professed representative of the unlawful association." This is the government that said there is terrorism and there is an uprising that is going to overthrow democracy. But each and every one of them will be turning against his constituents in voting against this amendment; there is no question about that. The minister drags out the five-year trial ban on capital punishment that was put into effect in December of 1967. We know that on that particular date the whips were on. But that does not necessarily apply to this act, because the bill before us is to provide temporary emergency powers for the preservation of public order within Canada.
There is no question in my mind that 70 per cent, 80 per cent, 90 per cent of the people of Canada believe that if a person is prepared to commit treason, to kill and torture human beings, good, law abiding Canadian citizens, he should receive the maximum penalty of death. I leave it to the government to decide by what means capital punishment should be applied, whether it be by hanging, the gas chamber or whatsoever method may be decided upon.
There is no question in my mind that most of Canada wants this amendment accepted and that most members of the House want it accepted. It is a cowardly act of the government to try to slide this amendment under the carpet tonight by dragging out the Criminal Code and saying that capital punishment is on a five-year trial period, so this amendment does not apply. This is a temporary measure for the specific purpose of preserving public order in Canada.
There is no doubt in my mind that capital punishment is in fact a deterrent. The Minister of Justice was a great believer in the value of a deterrent when it came to introducing the breathalyzer test. He used the argument that a deterrent was very important for the purpose of safeguarding persons using public highways. Now he does not believe in the value of a deterrent. He would rather have soldiers standing at the corner of every street, guarding every public building in Montreal with loaded machine-guns in their hands and fingers on the trigger. Is that not a deterrent? You bet it is a deterrent-but it is one that affects every law abiding citizen as he walks by the soldier with his finger on the trigger.
This amendment would bring in an effective deterrent for anyone committing a murder or an act of treason in order to create public disorder in an emergency situation such as the one we are now experiencing.

November 10, 1970
Public Order Act, 1970
Everyone who votes against this amendment will be duly recorded and will not be forgotten in the minds of the public or in the minds of the members of this House because, as the government has testified, this is an emergency situation which needs emergency action. I know some of my friends in the Socialist party to my left do not believe in capital punishment, but they accept there is an emergency situation in Canada today. At least, I believe they do. They also accept the fact that at this time the government must have some extraordinary powers. Therefore, maybe as a temporary measure they would support this amendment.
I conclude by saying that 80 per cent or 90 per cent of the people of Canada would vote in favour of this amendment. There is no doubt in my mind that the day will come when Members of Parliament will be elected to speak as their consciences dictate and to speak for their constituents. They will not be buying party favours by kow-towing to the wishes of the cabinet. Maybe we are five or ten years away from that day, but I say the day will come when this House will be directed by the consciences of the people who are elected and not by the wishes of the almighty party in power or the wishes of the almighty Minister of Justice who is afraid to stand up and say to his party, "You can have a free vote on this issue. Vote the way your conscience tells you".

I trust he will not assume that some of us do not know that. I trust he will realize that we are aware of tax credits and of other ways in which a problem like this can be solved.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
In my question on Tuesday, November 3, I referred to certain anomalies. May I indicate very briefly three such anomalies. First I mention the gross unfairness that is involved in giving to some of our old age pensioners a guaranteed income supplement, the purpose of which is to bring their income up to a certain level, and then turning around and taking some of that income away by taxing that bit of extra money. The Parliamentary Secretary can tell me that this applies in some cases and not in others. I am concerned about the cases where it does apply. I am concerned about retired persons who have their position improved on the one hand and downgraded on the other. This must be corrected.
A second anomaly relates to the fact that persons 70 years of age and over are allowed an extra $500 income tax exemption which does not apply any longer at age 65; at least, it does not apply to anyone between 65 and 70 who is in receipt of old age security during any month in any calendar year. I know the arguments for and against all this, but the anomaly I would like to point out to the Parliamentary Secretary is clear and straight forward. There are people between the ages of 65 and 70 who have nothing else but their pension income-people who are retired, who are out of the labour market-and yet because they are in that age bracket their exemption level, for single persons, is only $1,000. On the other hand there are people over 70 years of age who have income other than the old age pension, even people who have income from employment or income from investment. There are some in that age bracket who might have quite a lot of income and yet they are permitted an extra $500; in other words, a total $1,500 exemption so far as income tax is concerned. This I think is quite unfair, and it ought to be corrected.
I also think it is an anomaly, or a case of adding insult to injury, that pensioners, people who are on fixed incomes, have no opportunity to get an increase in their income to cope with the rising cost of living, and yet it is argued that because rules must have general application they cannot get an extra tax exemption or an extra tax credit. Precisely because their income position is fixed, precisely because they are denied some of the advantages that are available to those who are in the labour market, I think there is a case for different tax treatment of those people who are retired, those people who are on pensions only. I urge the government to give favourable consideration to this situation.
I know I repeat myself when I say to the Parliamentary Secretary: Don't come back and give me that line about the unfairness of raising income tax exemption levels because it does more for the rich than for the poor. It can be done by a system of tax credits. These pensioners of ours, our retired people, are having a terribly rough time today. They have to wait for white papers and legislation and for all the time it takes the government to deal with these matters. I think pensioners should benefit both ways. I have argued on previous occasions in favour of increasing the old age security pension to $150 a month, and I shall continue to do so. They should also benefit through whatever can be done in the matter of tax changes in their favour.

I urge that there be tax rebates, special tax treatment and tax arrangements that will give them a bit of justice instead of the unfairnesses and anomalies they now face. Mr. Speaker, the position of these people is desperate. For God's sake, I hope the government will do something about it soon.

The other question relates also to the amendment and concerns the word "assistance". The wording reads:
-gives that other person any assistance with intent thereby to prevent, hinder or interfere with the apprehension, trial or punishment-
Has the minister contemplated the extent to which this goes? I suppose it would not cover a witness who is appearing for the accused, nor, hopefully, would it cover his counsel, although one never knows. But much of what the minister said referred to the fact that the onus is placed on the accused to prove something that would discredit the earlier evidence against him. I am concerned merely with the question of retroactivity, and I say with the greatest respect to the minister that in his argument he was indulging in semantic legalisms.
Clause 8 is not the clause that provides the offence. It is true that the offence is provided in clause 4, and instead of having clause 8 here the minister could easily have added clause 8 as part of clause 4. That, surely, is irrelevant. What is relevant is that clause 8 sets out the facts under which a person is proven to be a member of the unlawful association, and being a member of the unlawful association is an offence against this law. Therefore, when you have proved that the person is a member of the unlawful association by reference to acts which occurred before the association was unlawful, you are making the substantive offence retroactive, and no number of words and no way of arguing will change that situation.
If I can be held to be a member of the FLQ today by virtue of the fact that I attended some meetings five years ago, then the law substantively is retroactive or retrospective. Certainly the retroactivity is in relation to the evidence on which I may be convicted, but this division between fact and law in this kind of situation seems to me to be entirely barren. When the minister referred to the fact that in an ordinary criminal case you can go back to acts, or action or behaviour of the accused prior to the date on which he is alleged to have committed the offence, you are dealing with something that has always been an offence. It has always been a crime to conspire to commit murder or to commit kidnapping. If I am alleged to have committed that crime on a certain date, and there is evidence prior to that date of my behaviour related to the crime with which I am charged, then of course it is admissible-not as evidence of the
charge as set out in the particulars but as evidence of my behaviour supporting that charge.
But this is a new offence. Membership in this organization was not unlawful before October 16. Attending a meeting of this organization was not proof of an unlawful act before October 16, nor was communicating on behalf of this unlawful organization an act which proved membership in an unlawful organization. It is this referral back to what I may have done a long time ago that is offensive.

Mr. Chairman, there is a
good deal in this legislation which I find offensive. Perhaps there is little that is more offensive than the clause we are discussing. The decision to include a clause which would allow the police to arrest and charge people who have been members of a particular group or organization for some years and who perhaps a few weeks ago terminated that membership, all argument to the contrary, is something that is so unbelievable and unjust that I find it difficult to comprehend that any government would have the audacity to bring such a suggestion in legislative form before this House. I find it repugnant that members of this House should be expected to approve a clause of this bill which would establish guilt on a retroactive basis.
This clause states that membership of any nature in an organization that was not considered unlawful until a few weeks ago can constitute the necessary evidence with which to charge a person with a criminal offence. This is too strong and unpalatable to be justified on the ground of security in this country. Not only are we in effect stating that certain acts in the past which individuals may have committed, or certain statements which individuals may have made, are a crime, but in this legislation we are creating a new crime which is either membership in, support for or encouragement given to a particular movement.
This would be bad enough in itself in light of the traditions of this country, but the fact is that we have not yet been given evidence in these many days or weeks of debate concerning the nature of the FLQ and what in particular would constitute reasonable evidence in respect of a criminal offence in this respect. Certainly the minister did not offer to this House in the earlier discussion on clause 3, which was stood, nor in the subsequent debate on various other clauses any relevant information concerning the exact nature of what would constitute a crime in respect of the FLQ. I think he has not done it primarily because he is not able to do it.
In the first instance, the minister has not been able to define the exact nature of the FLQ for purposes of arrest, charge and conviction. Are we, then, to be asked to put ourselves in the completely unbelievable position of suggesting that attendance at meetings or earlier support for some aspects of this organization will constitute evidence that would convict one of a criminal offence? This really is an Alice in Wonderland situation. I am amazed at the audacity and the fictional kind of existence in which the minister and the government must live, when they would expect either members of this House or the people of the country to believe that the establishment of a clause establishing retroactivity is in the best interests of the country or in the best interests of dealing with the present difficulties in the province of Quebec.
November 16, 1970

Further, it is beyond me how we can in all justice expect to have the people of this country accept as fair legislation which calls for the establishment of criminal offences which when committed in the past were not criminal. By the simple passage of this clause in the bill we would in effect be telling the people that something they did in the past, which to the very best of their knowledge did not constitute a criminal offence, has now in fact become a crime.
It is possible that next year the government might decide that some other organization is in effect of a like nature to the FLQ, and that it would constitute a criminal offence to support that organization, not only now when the legislation becomes valid but perhaps 10, 15 or 20 years ago when it seemed to be no criminal offence to belong to or support a specific organization. It is incredible that we should be engaging in a discussion of such a proposal this evening. Although we certainly are dealing with an organization which is repugnant to almost 100 per cent of the population today, this does not set aside the possibility that some other day another government, or perhaps this government, will propose similar steps in respect of other organizations, other activities, other bodies and other beliefs or ideologies.
In this proposal we are asked to accept a presumption of guilt which strikes me as being contrary to everything I understand of our system of justice. A person will be called upon to prove that in his earlier association, which he may have terminated half dozen years ago, he has no longer maintained some kind of active interest or support. How in the name of heaven is an innocent individual before the courts expected to prove the nebulous assertion that he is no longer an active member or supporter of that particular organization?

Not only must we provide laws that are just and fair to the citizenry of this country; they must, above all else, appear to be just. If we are seen to be assenting here in this place to this kind of unjust precedent, we do no service to the remainder of the body of laws and statutes of this country. I urge the minister to reconsider the wording of this clause so as to strike out what I think is offensive both to the House and to the good common law of this country.

Yes, Mr. Chairman.
Public Order Act, 1970
The amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South would change subclause 3 as follows, if I seize the purport of his amendment. It would read: "a peace officer may arrest without warrant a person who he has reasonable and probable grounds to suspect is a member of the unlawful association". I want to say to him that the words we chose, namely the words "reason to suspect" were deliberately chosen. As I pointed out in my speech on second reading, particularly as recorded at page 883 of Hansard, clause 9 is a special measure which the government recognizes does not exist in the ordinary criminal law.
We are dealing with specific short term legislation to meet a specific purpose, namely to attempt to immobilize and render inefficient the FLQ. The requirement "to have reason to suspect" is less stringent than that contained in the Criminal Code which requires the existence of reasonable and probable grounds to believe that an indictable offence has been committed. I refer hon. members to section 435(a) of the Criminal Code. The amendment does not remove the word "suspect" in clause 9(l)(a), and I assume this was done deliberately. However, by doing it deliberately, the hon. member leaves us with a hybrid concept, neither "reason to suspect" nor "reasonable and probable grounds to believe", but "reasonable and probable grounds to suspect", I believe this would confuse the case law even more than it may be confused already as to what the words "reasonable and probable grounds" may mean.
In any event, the amendment is obviously designed to make the condition precedent to lawful arrest more stringent, and in the present circumstances the government does not favour that. We are of the view that the requirement "reason to suspect" is both necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. It is the equivalent of the requirement prescribed in the statutes, principally with regard to matters of national security. I refer to the Official Secrets Act. Section 10 of the act provides:
Every person who is found committing an offence under this Act, or who is reasonably suspected of having committed, or having attempted to commit, or being about to commit, such an offence, may be arrested without a warrant and detained by any constable or police officer.
I want to submit to the committee that hon. members should not be under any apprehension that the words "reason to suspect" means that a person can be arrested without grounds. In order to satisfy the requirement in clause 9 (1) (a) as it is now written, there must be a bona fide reason to suspect that a person is a member of the illegal or unlawful association. In the absence of any bona fide reason to suspect, the provision would not apply. In other words, because of the nature of the conspiracy, because of the difficulty of obtaining evidence, because of the clandestine nature of the conspiracy, we feel that the standard imposed on a peace officer to arrest should be lowered as it is under the Official Secrets Act from "reasonable and probable grounds to believe" to "reason to suspect". For this reason, we prefer to use the concept of reason and suspect rather than the hybrid concept which the hon. member has used

Today my leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), very ably outlined the steps which the government must take to stimulate the economy and make it possible for additional industrial activity to provide additional jobs for our people. Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal, in the few minutes which are available to me this afternoon, with one particular aspect of the problem facing us, and that is the difficult task of providing the jobs which we need in the underdeveloped areas of this country where unemployment is considerably higher than in the other parts of the country.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the best way to increase employment in such areas is to work out a means by which we can attract more manufacturing industry, which is, of course, by far the greatest employer of labour, to those areas. That, of course, raises the question, can this be done? The answer is yes. The other question, "Well then, how can that be brought about", I intend to deal with now.

We have the raw materials, the cheap power, the transportation, and the skilled manpower. Despite the introduction of the government's regional development program, persistent unemployment of around 10 per cent in the Atlantic provinces, in Quebec and in British Columbia shows very clearly that, with the exception of the larger cities in those areas, there has been far too little development of manufacturing industry which, as I said, is by far the greatest producer of employment. The design and engineering were inadequate as the basis for a properly operating plant, and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was eventually called upon to advance further financial help. A large additional amount was then spent on redesigning and reconstructing the project. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate during which will be discussed most particularly the possibility of checking poverty and of removing by the same token a social injustice now widespread in Canada. It was quite normal to discuss this matter in the present context, in view of the difficulties we are facing now.
It is clear that every responsible government has the duty to create a climate of confidence. Certainly, it is difficult to create such a climate when we know that about 30 per cent of the Canadian people now live in poverty. In the last few years, insecurity has become prevalent here in Canada as well as the deterioration of the social environment.
As far as young people are concerned, they refuse to identify themselves with society. How could they agree to it blindly? In fact they have lost confidence not only in Parliament but also in its individual members.
The difficulties we are facing now may be due to the rapid evolution we have undergone in the past few years. It seems that youth craves liberty very much. To my mind, it is not only by dictatorial legislation that we will succeed in establishing a new atmosphere of confidence. The mere passage of legislation will not endow our society with a better way of life than the one we are enjoying at the present time.
I believe that it is the responsibility of the government to adopt the measures likely to fulfil the aspirations of Quebecers and all other Canadians.

It might be advisable to convene, as soon as possible, a summit meeting made up of representatives of the federal and provincial governments and of labour and management associations. Such a meeting would enable responsible members to discuss our present problems. In my view, such a meeting is necessary because it would represent not only the interests of governments but also those of the Canadian community. In fact, it would be beneficial to everyone.
Has the government really tried to give, for instance, to the young people, that freedom they are craving for, and which is the product of an evolution experienced throughout the world and not only in Quebec or in other regions of Canada? Has the government done its utmost to enable them to find summer employment?
I know that we spend millions, and I would even say that this is wasted money in some cases, to allow a certain number of young people to find summer jobs. Some people have suggested the establishment of compulsory military service, thought I do not feel that through such a dictatorial law we could solve this problem or satisfy youth.
I have always considered that the majority of our young people are full of good faith and prepared to build a better Canada. I have thought that a disciplinary training service, with pay, would perhaps be required, or at least valuable. We could in this set up mix business with pleasure, as people often say, allow all young Canadians, over the summer period, to join voluntarily this training service which would give them a certain discipline and would train men for peaceful purposes instead of training soldiers to wage war.
But who would be responsible for that disciplinary service? Would it be the federal government or the provinces? I would be inclined to think that the federal government should make some funds available to the provinces anxious to make use of such a service, ensuring to those young people an income which would enable them to continue their studies while giving them the opportunity of attaining manliness, as we all wish.
Such a service should be voluntary, because we have to take into account businessmen and farmers who need their children during the summer to work at home. But a responsible government could, through such an initiative, enable each province to take advantage of such a service and would allow thousands of young people to earn an income sufficient to improve their education and also practice the elementary discipline to which we must all submit in this world.
Since this would be a voluntary service, it would allow young people to reach university level with an excellent record. Application of this program would not involve a much greater cost to the taxpayer, since the young people, having earned an adequate income during the summer, would not need to apply to provincial governments for scholarships.
This program would give us an opportunity really to assess our young people and to know exactly how many of them want, not merely training, but work, and the experience of earning a dollar and investing it in themselves and the community as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would respectfully recommend to the federal government that when the federal and provincial finance ministers meet in Ottawa on December 7 and 8 to compare notes on the economy and to exchange information on the economic prospects for the next year, the federal government initiate discussions with the provinces immediately on the unemployment situation. They should also discuss joint initiatives that the two levels of governments could take to meet the crisis situation of the jobless in Canada this winter. I understand that most provinces are willing, and indeed quite anxious, to take part in such discussions. I feel it is incumbent upon this government to initiate the studies with the provincial finance ministers when they meet here on December 7 and 8.
This winter Canadians appear to be facing the most severe unemployment crisis since the great depression of the 1930's. According to economists and people eminently qualified to speak on the subject, it is expected that one out of every ten Canadians in the country's labour force will be out of a job by March of next year. This is a very very serious prospect. Should this happen, 750,000 to 800,000 men and women and their families will be facing a bitter struggle for economic survival in the months ahead.

I am glad it contains that language because some of the suggestions I wish to make relate to a long term cure for unemployment. Since unemployment is not caused by one factor solely, the cure for unemployment also will not involve merely one factor. We must do a great many things if we wish to cure unemployment. I should like to talk for a few moments about some ideas I have for this long term cure.

The point of my question was this: I felt that we were adopting a scattered approach in our spending on research, and that we ought to concentrate. Since we do not have enough money to spend on all areas of research, we ought to concentrate on those areas that will be of greatest advantage to us. We ought to concentrate consciously on those areas of research in which we can compete with other countries effectively. We must concentrate on those resources and goods with which we can compete with other countries of the world. As I say, we cannot afford to indulge in research in all areas, so we had better specialize.

We know that clause 15 contains a paradox, in that Parliament has the right to extend the special powers beyond April 30, but only the government can shorten the period. This, as I have said, is wrong, because Parliament ought not to be placed in a position that is subordinate to the duly elected autocracy.

There must be, as I said, police excesses and injustices causing mental and physical anguish to those arrested on suspicion only. When those conditions exist, Parliament ought to invoke the right requested. The second condition involves the lack of demonstrable need, because of a return to normalcy in Quebec, that the civil rights of all Canadians which are unnecessarily being restricted should be withheld no longer. Under those conditions Parliament ought to avail itself of this right to end the special powers as unnecessary.

I do not think the minister ought to be congratulated for pontificating on what is obvious. Everybody knows that with special powers comes a corresponding loss of freedom. We know this. Mr. Speaker, since we are discussing a motion of a temporary character and that we will soon have the opportunity to consider at length the matter of textile products and the government policy on this subject, my remarks will be brief.

November 26, 1970

I hope, as does the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), that this motion, which covers merely an extension of the Order in Council up to November 1971, the expiry date of the Order in Council in respect of the surtax on some shirts, may be passed quickly, because the expiry date is drawing near.
Mr. Speaker, I support the measure passed by the government last June, in order to curb imports of shirts into Canada. As a matter of fact, this measure intends to help an important sector of the textile industry until such time as a new policy on textile products is put into effect as announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce here, toward the end of the last session.
We are keenly concerned with the problems facing the textile industry and we have discussed them time and again, in committee, with other members specially concerned with them, and we have, on several occasions, made representations to the responsible government authorities, after many discussions with industries and unions involved.
I can tell the minister that the new program announced has been, on the whole, favourably received by all concerned but, as in the case of all programs, we are reserving judgment until we can see how fast and efficiently it will be implemented.
As the minister indicated earlier, this measure will give shirt manufacturers some protection against massive imports from low-cost countries, or countries where industries are nationalized, until such time as the new Textile and Clothing Board, the membership of which was announced last October, has been able to study and examine the whole problem and subsequently make recommendations to the proper authorities as to steps required to standardize and streamline this industry which is vital for the country.
I know that the shirt industry has been particularly affected for about fifteen years by a constant, immoderate and inadmissible increase of imports which lately contributed to the closing down of a certain number of factories and put others in an unbearable situation.
But the measure which was adopted last June and whose effect will be extended by the passage of this motion was certainly well received by all shirtmakers who are struggling for survival.
I insist that we take as soon as possible all necessary steps to protect at last the textile industry against irresponsible imports and to ensure that this industry whose survival is essential for the economy of Canada and especially of Quebec goes in for short and long term planning.
It should be recalled that in the past we have outdone ourselves in welcoming textile products from developing or low-cost countries. For instance, in 1966, Canada imported, per capita, three times as many textile products as the United States and about twice as many as Great Britain, and this inflow has surely not decreased since.
Surtax on Shirt Imports
The shirt industry for several years now has had to face a major volume of imports which reached a peak in 1968 while decreasing to some extent in 1969. But the situation is still critical and we must take action if we care for the survival of at least part of the industry. Like others, the textile industry is in need of a long-term overall policy which will allow it to build-up and modernize accordingly, to contribute as it should to our economy, to create jobs, to pay taxes and, finally, to operate in the same manner as any other responsible Canadian industry.
I know that, at the present time, large investments are in abeyance pending a clearer situation and knowledge of what exact direction will be taken by the industry.
Textile plants are mainly located in centres where the economy needs stimulation, in rural areas especially, i.e. in rural areas of Quebec and Ontario, and in some parts of western Canada. It is urgent to implement the new program aimed at establishing a development structure and conditions liable to create a climate of confidence in which the textiles industry could invest, and also to undertake or carry on the manufacturing of products which could compete increasingly on the international market.
Mr. Speaker, it should not be forgotten that one person out of eight employed in manufacturing in Canada is employed in the textile industry and that, in Quebec, the textile and clothing industry supplies 20 per cent of the jobs in the manufacturing sector. It cannot be blamed for dragging its feet with regard to modernization, because our industry is one of the most advanced in the world, from the technological angle, and has not stopped investing to stay up to date. If the government applies in a quick, efficient and realistic manner the new policy announced by the minister, I am sure that this industry will continue its efforts to adapt to future markets and to contribute more to the progress of the Canadian economy.

When I began to study the resolution, I referred at once to the statutes of Canada, 1968-69. By looking at the last amendment which dealt with section 7 of the Customs Tariff, I came to the conclusion that this resolution is not legal.
Therefore, we had to refer to Bill C-140 passed during the 1969-70 session to see what was the procedure to follow regarding the acceptance of a resolution concerning the adoption of such an Order in Council. In view of the fact that it has become the usual practice for Parliament to adjourn at the end of June until October, as was the case this year, the printing and binding of statutes stop then. Nobody, except those familiar with Parliament who might have a copy of legislation passed during the last session, would be able to check to see whether or not the resolution is legal and to advise their customers accordingly.

November 26, 1970
Surtax on Shirt Imports
After all, the minister must know that several importers have shirts in their warehouses waiting perhaps for the Order in Council to expire or to be continued in eifect through the adoption of the resolution under consideration.
For instance, if a Vancouver lawyer had to advise an importer, he could not tell him whether it is true or not, and in what way he should act, because he would not have the Statutes of Canada for 1969-1970.
That is why I say it is all very well to adjourn the House from June until October, but we should not stop the publication of the statutes passed during the year. The statutes adopted during the previous session are not yet published. I suggest that the House administration services look into this problem, since it affects the people's rights.
It is easy for people from Ottawa or Montreal to meet their representative in the House and to seek his advice, but it is not so easy for those living outside Ottawa or Montreal. I urge the Chair to consider the possibility of taking remedial action.

Four provinces require the same notice for quits as for dismissals. Ontario provides for partial reciprocity, but the notice periods are considerably less for employees. The hon. member for Calgary North has filed a notice of his intention to propose a motion under Standing Order 26. I have given very serious consideration to the matter and have considered all the procedural aspects of the motion. The hon. member for Calgary North proposes that the business ordered for today be set aside so that the House may debate Treasury Board decision affecting the remuneration of senior officials of the Auditor General's office, going back to July 1, 1967. The hon. member charges that the efficiency of the Auditor General's office has been impaired as a result of such action by Treasury Board.
Hon. members know the criteria which must guide the Chair in relation to Standing Order 26. I must determine whether the subject matter sought to be discussed can be termed an emergency. The word "emergency" used in relation to Standing Order 26 has always been interpreted to refer to a sudden occurrence, a newly arising situation which, because of that aspect, requires the immediate, urgent consideration of the House.
Is this requirement met in the circumstances indicated by the hon. member for Calgary North? This is obviously a very important matter and one which is or should be of interest and concern to all hon. members; and there is an aspect of immediacy in the sense that relevant evidence has just been heard by the public accounts committee. On the other hand, the situation referred to in the proposed motion goes back to July, 1967.
It is hardly necessary to remind the House that the Auditor General's relation to the government has been brought to the attention of the House on a number of occasions in recent months. In particular, the matter was raised on April 6 last by the hon. member for Peace River, also under the provisions of Standing Order 26. On April 13 the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands again brought the situation to the attention of the House, at that time by way of a question of privilege. The hon. member's motion is based on a submission that there was an attempt to "harass and intimidate the Auditor General".
Motions for Papers
The Chair also has to take into account the possibility that the matter might be debated in other circumstances. The House has before it at the present time the bill that was referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Peace River. The Auditor General's report is now before the Public Accounts Committee and it can be reasonably assumed by the Chair that in due course the committee's report will be debated in the House. What is perhaps even more relevant is that the budget debate will take place very soon. While I agree the matter is an important and urgent one which hon. members may wish to debate, for all these reasons I suggest such a debate should take place as part of a discussion on a substantive motion rather than within the somewhat limited framework provided under Standing Order 26.

The purpose of the tour was to provide heads of mission accredited to the Government of Canada with an opportunity to see at first hand something of the Canadian north and the developments taking place there. However, this is certainly one which we can look upon with sympathy and understanding. He has zeroed in on a problem that is well recognized. It is one of the major problems in our increasingly urbanized society.
One of the outstanding lessons in this century is that the capacity of our environment to decompose waste materials to harmless levels is not infinite. While the ability of the environment to assimilate our wastes is finite, the production of wastes is accelerating as we aspire to newer amenities and ways of life. We are rapidly overtaking the capacity of our environment to handle the waste that our way of life generates.
A diseased environment, such as results from the conditions described by the hon. member, means distress to all of us in a variety of ways. This extends beyond the

physical well-being of man. It proliferates into the psycho-social and economic realms, not to mention the delayed, subtle impact on the ecology of our earth which sustains human life as we know it today. Granting that human activities must result in residues, and granting that all these residues will not be useful, or capable of being decomposed by nature, there is a real need, as the hon. member has suggested, to define both the nature and the momentum of the danger facing our society, to identify existing and potential hazards, and to develop a strategy to control them.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address the minister responsible to Parliament for the Canadian Wheat Board in the hope that I might clarify the question I directed to the minister in the oral question period on December 11.
